questions.question: Positive Therapy suggests that the search for Empirically Validated Therapies (EVTs) has been handcuffed by its focus on------ a). Focusing on making 'normal people stronger' rather than 'miserable people less miserable. b). Validating the effect of building strengths like optimism and perseverance. c). Validating specific techniques that repair damage and map uniquely into DSM-IV categories. d). Over-relying on the non- specifics like rapport and trust. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Subjective Level, it investigates internal, positive states like happiness, joy, life satisfaction, and positive
  • emotions (e.g., love, contentment), as well as constructive thoughts such as optimism and hope. 2. The
  • Individual Level focuses on stable, positive individual traits and enduring behavior patterns,
  • encompassing character strengths or virtues like courage, honesty, persistence, and wisdom, alongside
  • the pursuit of excellence and creative potential. 3. Finally, the Society/Group Level examines the
  • development and maintenance of positive institutions, addressing issues critical to collective
  • flourishing, such as civic virtues, creating healthy families, and fostering positive communities and
  • work environments.
  • The scope of positive psychology is vast, applying its principles and research to promote well-being and
  • flourishing across three main levels: the Individual Level (e.g., personal growth, resilience,
  • relationships), the Group and Organizational Level (e.g., positive organizations, education, family
  • systems), and the Community and Societal Level (e.g., informing public policy, building positive
  • communities, and integrating into therapy).Scope: Application in education, therapy, workplace, and
  • community well-being.

questions.solution_html:

  • as optimism and resilience, to act as a buffer against mental illness and to enhance overall well-being.

  • evidence based techniques, promoting and flourishing.

questions.question: Define the concept of "Meaningful Life". / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Meaningful life: A life in which an individual finds purpose, coherence, and significance
  • beyond mere happiness, often linked to eudaimonia, achieved by using signature strengths and virtues
  • in the service of something much larger than the person himself. It involves aligning one’s actions with
  • values, nurturing relationships, and contributing to something beyond self, which promotes overall well-
  • being and a sense of lasting satisfaction.

questions.question: Why is forgiveness considered a crucial concept for society? / [CO4]

  • reduces interpersonal and group conflicts, and fosters emotional healing and reconciliation. It facilitates
  • social cohesion, and breaks destructive cycles of hurt and retaliation. It provides a foundation for justice

questions.question: Define Human Flourishing and explain how it broadens the scope beyond simple happiness. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Define Human Flourishing and explain how it broadens the scope beyond simple happiness:
  • Human flourishing is defined as a state of living "within an optimal range of human functioning" that
  • encompasses a holistic sense of well-being and fulfillment across multiple dimensions of life, not
  • merely simple happiness. It is an active, ongoing process of developing one's capabilities, strengths, and
  • virtues, it includes optimal functioning in life domains such as meaning, relationships, and personal
  • growth. PERMA model explains this. PERMA stands for Positive emotions, Engagement,
  • Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment, and these elements are crucial for a fulfilling and
  • flourishing life

questions.question: Explain the characteristics of hedonic happiness. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Characteristics of hedonic happiness: Focus on pleasure attainment and pain avoidance,
  • immediate gratification, and positive affect. Key characteristics include a focus on immediate
  • gratification from sensory pleasures (like good food), external validation (like fame or money), and
  • short-lived bursts of fun rather than long-lasting fulfillment.

questions.question: How does Ryff’s model differ from Diener’s SWB model? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Ryff’s model vs Diener’s SWB model: Ryff emphasizes psychological well-being with
  • multiple dimensions; Diener focuses on subjective well-being emphasizing affect and life satisfaction.
  • Diener's model defines well-being from a subjective, "hedonic" perspective focused on happiness and
  • pleasure, It leaves the definition of a good life up to the individual's own subjective judgment. Focus is
  • maximizing pleasure and happiness while minimizing pain and negative emotions. It is about "feeling
  • good. Components- Life Satisfaction, Positive Affect and Negative Affect. while Ryff's model defines
  • it from an "eudaimonic" perspective focused on objective psychological functioning and self-
  • realization. It is rooted in developmental and humanistic psychology and focuses on the realization of
  • human potential. Optimal psychological functioning and personal growth. It suggests there are
  • objective, universal criteria for a good life. t has six distinct dimensions: Autonomy, Environmental
  • Mastery, Personal Growth, Positive Relations with Others, Purpose in Life and Self-Acceptance.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does self-concept differ from self-esteem? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Self-concept vs self-esteem: Self-concept is the cognitive understanding of oneself; self-
  • esteem is the evaluative and emotional appraisal of self-worth. Self-concept is a collection of beliefs
  • about One’s self, whereas self-esteem is the feeling of self-worth and value derived from those beliefs.

questions.question: Explain how a person can use grateful reappraisal to cope with a painful memory from the past. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Grateful reappraisal for coping with painful memory:
  • Grateful reappraisal is a cognitive restructuring technique that transforms the meaning of a negative
  • event. It shifts the focus from the suffering caused by the memory to the subsequent benefits or strengths
  • gained.Using gratitude to reinterpret past negative experiences positively, focusing on lessons learned and
  • personal growth, thereby reducing distress.
  • • Acknowledge the Pain, Then Shift Focus: The process doesn't involve minimizing the
  • original hurt or trauma. Instead, the individual first acknowledges the pain associated with the memory,
  • but then deliberately directs their thoughts to what good has since emerged.
  • • Identify Benefits and Lessons: The person systematically asks questions regarding the
  • lessons learned, how can the person become stronger, development of new relationship, career path or
  • new belief, preventive measures, and the outcomes of it to re-examine the event's lasting impact.
  • • By finding these positive results (e.g., increased empathy, greater resilience, a deeper
  • appreciation for current peace, finding one's life purpose), the individual is essentially reframing the
  • painful memory not as a purely destructive force, but as a catalyst for positive change and growth.
  • • Cultivate Gratitude: The final step is actively feeling gratitude for those new strengths or
  • positive consequences. This changes the emotional valence of the memory—while the memory remains
  • painful, the overall emotional experience linked to it is now tempered with thankfulness for the resulting
  • wisdom or benefit. Can include an example also
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the role of Life Enhancement Strategies in various settings. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Life Enhancement Strategies in various settings: These strategies for boosting well-being and
  • happiness draw heavily from the PERMA Model (Positive Emotion, Engagement, Relationships,
  • Meaning, Accomplishment) and encompass actionable techniques across seven key areas. Individuals
  • can cultivate Positive Emotions through practices like gratitude journaling, savouring positive
  • experiences, and mindfulness meditation. Engagement (Flow) is increased by identifying and
  • deliberately using signature strengths in daily life and pursuing optimal challenges that match skill with
  • difficulty. Positive Relationships are nurtured by using Active-Constructive Responding to good news,
  • performing acts of kindness, and prioritizing quality time with loved ones. Finding Meaning and
  • Purpose involves clarifying core values, aligning actions with those values, and contributing to
  • something larger than oneself. Accomplishment is boosted by setting SMART goals, celebrating small
  • wins, and maintaining a growth mindset. Additionally, maintaining Physical Well-being through regular
  • exercise, a healthy diet, and sufficient sleep is crucial. Finally, effective Cognitive Strategies include
  • fostering optimism, using positive reappraisal to constructively reframe events, and practicing self-
  • compassion in the face of setbacks.
  • The practical application of positive psychology strategies is wide-ranging, addressing well-being and
  • flourishing across various sectors. For Individual Self-Improvement, these tools, such as mindfulness
  • and gratitude, are used daily for stress management, personal development, and increasing resilience
  • against adversity. In Clinical and Counselling Settings, methods are integrated into Positive
  • Psychotherapy and coaching to not only alleviate distress but also actively build client strengths.
  • Education (Positive Education) implements programs to teach students and train teachers in practices
  • like gratitude and character strengths to foster student flourishing and academic success. Workplaces
  • (Positive Organizations) utilize these strategies to boost employee well-being, engagement, and
  • productivity through initiatives like strengths-based leadership and connecting work to a broader
  • purpose. At the level of Family and Relationships, interventions strengthen bonds through practices like
  • active-constructive responding and positive parenting. Finally, on a broader scale, Public Health and
  • Policy is increasingly incorporating well-being indicators to inform policy decisions and design
  • community interventions that promote social connection and mental health.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the Broaden-and-Build Theory of Positive Emotions and explain its applications in education, workplace, and therapy. / [CO3] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Broaden-and-Build Theory and applications:
  • • Theory: Positive emotions broaden awareness and build enduring personal resources. The
  • Broaden-and-Build Model of Positive Emotions, proposed by Barbara Fredrickson, explains how
  • positive emotions fundamentally contribute to personal growth and long-term well-being. It posits two
  • key hypotheses that distinguish positive emotions (like joy, interest, and serenity) from negative ones
  • (which narrow focus for survival). The Broaden Hypothesis states that positive emotions temporarily
  • expand ("broaden") our momentary thought-action repertoires, making us more creative, flexible, and
  • open to new ideas and experiences. The subsequent Build Hypothesis asserts that this broadened
  • mindset allows individuals to actively accumulate ("build") enduring personal resources over time,
  • including physical (e.g., coordination), intellectual (e.g., knowledge), social (e.g., relationships), and
  • psychological (e.g., resilience) assets. This process creates an "upward spiral," where positive emotions
  • lead to the building of resources, which in turn enhances well-being, making future positive emotions
  • more likely.
  • Applications: Enhancing creativity and resilience in education, improving employee well-being and
  • productivity in workplaces, and supporting therapeutic change. Challenges the "Hedonic Treadmill":
  • Provides a scientific explanation for why positive emotions are more than just momentary pleasures;
  • they are crucial for growth. Basis for Positive Interventions: Many positive psychology interventions
  • (e.g., gratitude practices, mindfulness, savouring, cultivating kindness) are designed to evoke positive
  • emotions precisely because of their broadening and building effects. Resilience: Explains how positive
  • emotions (even in difficult times) can help individuals bounce back from adversity by building adaptive
  • coping mechanisms. Organizational and Educational Settings: Encourages fostering positive emotions
  • to enhance creativity, teamwork, learning, and employee engagement.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
